checked: src/Scans/*.jl (grepped: zero docstrings, confirmed out of the ?name surface)

findings.title: 'consumer' and 'pin' are used, undefined, in the very first sentences a REPL reader sees
locations: src/GBGCodingTools.jl:5-6: "...at one version pinned by every consumer. A consumer holds data; the tool holds behaviour; the only thing connecting them is a pin."
findings.description: `?GBGCodingTools` is the first thing a cold reader of this package types, and its module docstring — the map RULE.DOC.MODULE_MAP calls for — opens with two of the package's own terms of art, 'consumer' and 'pin', used as bare nouns with no gloss and no @ref. Both are defined only in the external policy prose (glossary.md, ARCHITECTURE.md §0), which the substrate rule of this lane withholds and which is not part of the docstring surface a `?name` session ever loads. I grepped every docstring in src/ and ext/ for a defining sentence for 'consumer' ("a package that pins the tool", "the four GBG packages", etc.) and found none: the word is used in dozens of docstrings (DocLints.jl, TestHarness.jl, Config.jl, Git.jl, Ledger.jl, Sync.jl, Doctor.jl, Init.jl...) but never once explained. A reader who has not read ARCHITECTURE.md has no way to know a 'consumer' is one of the four sibling GBG packages (or the tool testing itself) rather than, say, an end user of the reviewed package's API.
findings.resolution_hint: Add one clause to the GBGCodingTools module docstring that states what a consumer is (e.g. "— a consumer is one of the sibling GBG Julia packages, or the tool testing itself —") and, separately, state what a pin is in plain terms before using it as a bare noun; RULE.DOC.TERMS_DEFINED requires the definition at first use, not a later page.

findings.title: TestHarness's 'element-traffic ledger' collides with the package's own defined term 'Ledger'
locations: src/TestHarness.jl:183: "One row of the traffic ledger." (the `audit` docstring)
findings.description: 'Ledger' is one of the package's ten declared terms of art (config: package.terms), with one fixed meaning stated in Ledger.jl's own module docstring: 'the reader of a consumer's exemption ledger `.gbg/exemptions.toml`'. TestHarness.jl reuses the ordinary English word 'ledger' for a completely different mechanism — the CountingArray/Traffic/audit read-write bookkeeping — in its module docstring, a section header and the `audit` docstring itself. A cold reader who has already formed 'ledger = the exemptions file' from Ledger.jl (or from the package's own terms list) hits 'the element-traffic ledger' in TestHarness and must silently discard that referent and build a second, unrelated one — exactly the failure mode the lane brief calls out: an ordinary word carrying a package-specific meaning is overloaded with a second, conflicting package-specific meaning.
findings.resolution_hint: Rename the TestHarness concept (e.g. 'the traffic audit' or 'the traffic table', mirroring `traffic_completeness`/`AUDITED_TRAFFIC_OPS`) so 'ledger' stays bound to one referent across the whole package, per RULE.DOC.ONE_NOTATION's 'one notation per concept' applied to prose terms.

findings.title: 'S-class' and 'class G' file-taxonomy letters are used in docstrings but defined nowhere in them
locations: src/CLI/Init.jl:11 (module docstring): "`init` never renders the G files: that is `gbg sync`"
src/CLI/Sync.jl:189 (`plan` docstring): "Every generated-managed file (class G) for a consumer"
src/CLI/Init.jl:450 (`migrate_baselines` docstring): "the textual converter from the consumer's existing test files to the three S-class TOMLs `TestHarness` reads"
findings.description: The package apparently classifies its managed/generated files by letter (at least G and S appear), a taxonomy that lives in ARCHITECTURE.md — withheld from a cold read — but never in any exported docstring. 'class G' is used once with a one-word gloss ('generated-managed'), which a reader could just about hold onto; but 'S-class' in Init.jl's `migrate_baselines` docstring is used with zero gloss at all, and by then the reader has no earlier anchor for the letter scheme (I grepped every docstring in src/ and ext/ for 'class [A-Z]' or '[A-Z]-class' and found only these three lines, none of which explains the scheme). A competent reader new to the package cannot recover what distinguishes an S-class file from a G-class one, or how many other letters exist.
findings.resolution_hint: Either drop the bare letter and say what the class means in the sentence itself ('the three frozen TOML baselines' instead of 'the three S-class TOMLs'), or add one sentence to a central docstring (e.g. Sync's or Init's module doc) naming the classes that appear anywhere in the exported surface.

findings.title: 'substrate' is used as a field name across three files before it is ever explained as a concept
locations: src/CLI/Recall.jl:9 (module docstring, first docstring use): "[`Recall.suspect_hats`](@ref) names the hats with two or more seeds on their substrate and zero matches"

src/CLI/Preflight.jl:167-169 (`resolve_hats`): "Each hat carries `key`, `substrate`, `needs`, `anchor`... and `not_applicable` when its substrate cannot exist here (`html` needs with no built site, `git` with no repository, `rulebook` with no rulebook sections)."
findings.description: 'Substrate' denotes which manuscript view a hat is shown (full manuscript, site-only manuscript, or the built HTML), but that is never stated as a definition anywhere — it must be reverse-engineered from the enumerated example values ('full', 'siteonly', 'html', 'scans' as seen in Passes.jl and Init.jl) scattered across Recall.jl, Preflight.jl, Rounds.jl and Passes.jl. Recall.jl's module docstring — the first docstring to use the word — gives no gloss at all ('their substrate' reads as though the concept is already known). This is exactly an ordinary English word (substrate = the material something sits on) repurposed for a specific, closed-vocabulary field whose values are never listed in one place.
findings.resolution_hint: State once, at Preflight.resolve_hats (the docstring with the richest context) or in the Preflight module docstring, that 'substrate' names which manuscript/build view a hat is shown (full | siteonly | html | scans), then let later uses rely on the @ref.

findings.title: 'round' is used as load-bearing vocabulary in the first files a reader loads, well before any docstring characterizes it
locations: src/Witnesses.jl:179 (`run`'s docstring, 7th file in the module's own include order): "`dir` — the directory of `.jl` witnesses (the round's `witnesses/`, or `test/regressions/escalated/`)"
src/CLI/Self.jl:49 (`self_verify`'s docstring): "an edited pinned tree is never allowed to grade a round"
findings.description: 'Round' is one of the package's ten declared terms of art. It is used as settled vocabulary in Witnesses.jl (bare 'the round's witnesses/') and again in Self.jl, both of which load well before RoundFiles.jl — the first module whose docstring gives round any structure at all ('round_dirs', 'ROUND.toml', the :open/:closed/:abandoned states) — and even RoundFiles.jl never states the one-line definition the glossary gives ('one run of an instrument, recorded as a tracked directory under .gbg/rounds/'); it only shows the reader mechanics. A reader proceeding through the package in its own include/documentation order meets 'round' as an assumed concept several files before encountering enough structure to construct a definition, and never meets an explicit one.
findings.resolution_hint: Add a one-clause definition of 'round' to the Witnesses module docstring (its first use) or promote RoundFiles's module docstring earlier / add an explicit definitional sentence to it rather than only operational description.

findings.title: 'anchor' (a hat/lane running at full strength) is never defined in any docstring
locations: src/CLI/Preflight.jl:167 (`resolve_hats`): "Each hat carries `key`, `substrate`, `needs`, `anchor` (a `domain_hats` entry may anchor any key)"
src/CLI/Doctor.jl:281: `push!(errs, "no anchored hat (at least one hat runs at full strength)")` — a runtime error string, not a docstring, so a `?name` reader never sees it
findings.description: 'Anchor' is one of the package's ten declared terms of art, glossed in policy as 'a hat or lane that runs at full strength instead of the economy model'. In the docstring surface it appears only as an opaque boolean field name ('anchor' in a Dict, 'anchored' as a parenthetical) with no sentence anywhere stating what being anchored means. The one place the concept is spelled out in English ('at least one hat runs at full strength') is a doctor check's failure message in Doctor.jl, which lives in executable code, not a docstring — invisible to `?Preflight.resolve_hats` or any other `?name` lookup.
findings.resolution_hint: State the meaning of `anchor` once in resolve_hats's or resolve_roster's docstring (e.g. "`anchor` — whether this hat/lane runs at full strength rather than the economy model") since that is where the field is first introduced to a reader.

findings.title: 'managed file' (a defined package term) is used pervasively via 'managed' but never stated as a concept
locations: src/CLI/Sync.jl:8-12 (module docstring): "Renders and checks the managed footprint of a consumer: the skill stubs, ... and the sidecar `.gbg/managed.json`."
findings.description: 'Managed file' is one of the package's own glossary terms ('a file the tool renders into a consumer and hash-checks thereafter; edited only by `gbg sync`'). Sync.jl's module docstring and every function under it (`plan`, `status`, `sync`, `ManagedFile`, `Entry`) use 'managed' as an adjective dozens of times, and a reader can infer a good deal from the mechanics shown (STALE/MODIFIED/OK states, hash comparison), but no docstring anywhere states the concept in one sentence the way the glossary does — a reader must assemble the definition themselves from `classify`, `classify_block` and the `Entry` struct's field docs rather than being told directly.
findings.resolution_hint: Add one defining clause to the Sync module docstring, e.g. "a managed file is one this tool renders and hash-checks; a consumer never hand-edits it", ahead of the mechanics.

findings.title: the act/state verdict channels, and the 'class_surfaces' field that demotes one, are used before (and largely without) explanation
locations: src/CLI/Demote.jl:6-7 (`demote`'s docstring, the field's only appearance anywhere in the source): "an act verdict `HONORED` whose `class_surfaces` is empty becomes `LINE-ONLY`"
src/CLI/Passes.jl:121: "Launch BOTH verifiers exactly as printed (the act verifier sees the diff; the state verifier is blind)"
findings.description: Demote.jl's `demote` — an early file in the closure-verification group — is the first and only docstring anywhere to use 'act verdict' and 'class_surfaces'; neither is glossed there. 'act' versus 'state' as the two verification channels only gets any contrasting explanation four files later, in Passes.jl's `pass_open` ('the act verifier sees the diff; the state verifier is blind'), and even that never says what the act/state SPLIT is for (checking whether a claimed fix landed, versus whether the underlying defect is now absent). `class_surfaces` — the field the whole `demote` rule turns on — appears nowhere else in the entire source tree (grepped), so a reader has no way to learn what it is meant to hold beyond 'a list that, when empty, demotes the verdict'.
findings.resolution_hint: Expand `demote`'s docstring with one clause on what 'act' means (as opposed to 'state') and what class_surfaces records (the surfaces the finding's own text names as swept, per RULE.DOC.CLASS_SWEEP), since this is the field's only documented occurrence.
